messages.author: 0839befa8a8b7d53
messages.subject: Re: We Need You!
parts:
I am an evolutionary anthropologist. I have two manuscripts in the wild that used Stan for modeling.

(1) An analysis of serotonin receptor variation and behavior, using Stan for some ordered logit models. Nothing fancy, just nice to have solid convergence with arbitrary varying effect structures. Also, ordered logit in Stan has been much faster for me than doing it in JAGS, I assume because of the awkward intermediate nodes needed in a JAGS implementation (?). This paper is in press at PNAS, so embargoed, but I could forward the citation along, once I have page numbers.

(2) A paper on human foraging returns across the lifespan, using multilevel gamma regressions with imputation. Most complex models have tens-of-thousands of parameters. Stan has saved my bacon, here. This paper is under review.

On the experimental end, I've gotten Stan to do a nice job on dynamic social learning data. The models are variants of "experience weighted attraction" models, with varying effects added. These models work much nicer in Stan than in other engines I've tried, I think because all of the calculations that go into computing the "attraction" scores get compiled down to lean C++ code in Stan, so aren't interpreted during sampling.

I also wrote a convenience R package, glmer2stan, to generate basic GLMM Stan models from lme4-style model formulas. This has been useful in teaching, mainly. I've been meaning to migrate it's repository over to github. So once Rstan appears there, I'll see about linking it up.

messages.author: 4cef6eb14d12f9f6
messages.subject: Re: We Need You!
parts:
I'm using Stan to model electricity use vs time in commercial buildings. There are several applications. My main interests at the moment are:
1. Creating a "baseline model" to predict how much electricity a building will use over a short time interval (such as 4 to 6 hours) under business as usual. An intervention is then performed that lasts a few hours, and the question is, how much energy did the intervention save? We subtract the actual energy from the predicted energy to get an estimate of this. My models use time-of-day and time-of-week indicator variables, plus a non-linear temperature response, plus an autoregressive noise term. All parameters can change from one week to the next, but there are constraints about the changes (based on prior knowledge of how building schedules work). 
2. Detecting faults and anomalies. Week-to-week changes in parameters (such as the relationship between outdoor air temperature and electricity consumption, at a given time of day) should usually be small; a big increase usually means something has gone wrong.

The usual approaches to these problems are quite simplified. With Stan I can fit a model that is much closer to describing the way a building really works (for instance, some schedule changes affect every weekday; others affect only certain days of the week; and if a change affects one 15-minute interval then it probably affects the subsequent one as well; and so on). 

My biggest problem is speed: it takes hours for my model to run on a realistically useful amount of data (say, 10 weeks of data collected every 15 minutes), which makes extending it and testing it a very slow process. But it's much much better than any alternative I know of. 

Phil Price
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory

Yes, that sounds like you could fit it with Stan.  Do you have a BUGS/JAGS model to start from?  Or a mathematical definition of the full probability function?

Because of Stan's imperative nature, it's easy to fit things like zero-inflated Poisson models.  I just revised our appendix to match the definition in (Lambert 1992) of zero-inflated Poisson distributions.

I've attached a PDF of the revised manual page.

- Bob
